excerpt: The path from a cable in the ground to a page on your screen: the line, the router, the provider, and why the whole street can be slow at once.

body.text: This lesson follows the internet from the street to your screen. You will learn what the cable, the router, and the provider each do, and why a fault in one place affects everybody at once.
The internet arrives through one line, which may be fibre, a phone line, or a mobile signal. Everything in the house shares that line, which explains most of the slow evenings.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
A look at the box where the line enters the house.

body.text: The path, in order

items: A fibre or copper cable reaches the building, often through a small box on the wall.
The cable connects to the provider's equipment, which may be the router itself.
The router gives each device in the house an address and shares the line.
The provider connects the building to its own network and then to the wider internet.
Names are translated to addresses along the way, which is how a word becomes a page.
Every device in the house competes for the same line.

body.text: You will see a small box on the wall with a thin cable entering it, usually near a window or under the stairs. That box is where the provider's responsibility ends and yours begins.

body.alt: A thin fibre cable entering a small box on a wall.
body.caption: The thin cable at the wall. Do not bend or cut it, since a fibre strand breaks rather than bends.

body.text: It looks like a slow connection is the provider's fault alone. Ten devices on one line slow each other down, and that is a fact about the house rather than the network.
What the provider controls

items: The line from the street to the building, and the speed it is set to.
The network beyond the building, including the busy hours.
The address your house presents to the outside world.
The maintenance that causes planned outages.
The support line and the fault ticket.
The price and the bundle, which change what is possible.

body.text: A fault report will give you a ticket number and sometimes a promised date. Keep both, since the number is how a second call becomes a follow-up rather than a fresh complaint.

The provider's status page will show your line with a green tick or a warning, and that screen is worth a screenshot before you call. A picture of the current status is faster than describing the fault from memory.

body.alt: A telecom mast against an evening sky.
body.caption: The mast carries the mobile half of the network. Its signal shares the same backhaul as the wired line.

body.text: What you control
Inside the building, everything belongs to you, and most everyday problems live there.

items: Where the router sits, which decides how far the signal reaches.
How many devices are connected, and what they are doing.
The wifi password, and who has it.
The cables, which fail at the plug more often than in the middle.
The devices themselves, which can be the slow part.
The habits, such as downloading films at eight in the evening.

body.text: None of this needs the provider. Moving a router, changing a password, and closing an old download solve more complaints than any support call.
Do not worry about understanding the whole chain. Knowing where your responsibility ends is enough to ask the right question.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a first check, and the first check decides who to call.

items: The whole street is down: report it and wait, since nothing inside the house will fix it.
One device fails and the rest work: the problem is the device, not the line.
Everything fails after a storm: check the wall box and call the provider.
Slow only in the evening: the network is busy. Schedule downloads for the morning.
The line works and the wifi does not: restart the router before calling anybody.
A cable is damaged near the door: report it, since a customer repair can break the fibre.

body.text: Practice
Find the wall box and learn one number.

items: Find where the line enters the house.
Photograph the wall box and the router's label.
Note the provider's support number and your account number.
Count the devices connected to the wifi.
Ask one neighbour whether their connection is slow at the same hour.

body.text: You can now see the whole path a page travels. In the next lesson you will read the five lights on the router.

excerpt: What each light on a home router means, the restart order that fixes most faults, and where to put the box so the signal reaches the rooms you use.

body.text: This lesson explains the lights on a home router and the restart that fixes most problems. You will learn what each light means, the order to switch things off and on, and where the box should sit.
A router is a small computer with a modem inside. The lights are its way of telling you which part is working, and reading them takes ten seconds.
Before you start

items: The router, and a moment to look at it.
The provider's support number.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: The five lights

items: Power: solid when the router has electricity.
Internet or globe: solid when the provider's line is working.
DSL or WAN: solid when the line is connected, flashing while it trains.
Wifi: solid or flashing when the wireless signal is on.
LAN: one light per cable port, lit when a cable is connected.
Any light that is red, or off when it should be on, is the one to report.

body.text: You will see the internet light go off during an outage, while the power and wifi lights stay on. That pattern tells you the fault is outside the house.

The router's settings page will show the connection state as connected or disconnected, with an uptime figure beside it. A short uptime that keeps resetting means the line is dropping and reconnecting.
The wifi menu will open with a list of every device attached, each with a name and an address. Reading that list is how you find the guest who never left, and the device somebody forgot to remove.

body.alt: A home router on a wooden shelf with several indicator lights.
body.caption: Read the lights before calling anybody. The internet light alone explains most of the calls made to a provider.

body.text: It looks like a red light means the router is broken. A red internet light usually means the provider's line is down, which the router cannot fix.
The restart that works
The order matters, which is why a quick switch off and on often does nothing.

items: Switch the router off at the wall and unplug it.
Wait thirty seconds, which lets the provider's side notice the disconnection.
Plug it in and switch on, then wait two minutes without touching it.
Watch the lights come on in order, ending at the internet light.
Test one page on one device before trying everything.
Repeat once only, since a third attempt changes nothing.

body.text: The lights will settle in a sequence, and the internet light is the last to stop flashing. Until it is steady, nothing in the house will load, so waiting is part of the fix.

body.alt: Hands switching a router off at the wall socket.
body.caption: Off at the wall, thirty seconds, then on. The pause is what makes the restart work.

body.text: Where the box should sit

items: Put it high and central, not shut in a cabinet or behind a television.
Keep it away from a microwave, which interferes while it runs.
Keep it away from water and from the floor, where it collects dust.
Do not stack books on it, since the vents need air.
Point the antennae upward if it has them.
Put it where you can see the lights, which saves a walk during every fault.

body.text: None of this needs a new router. Position and a restart fix the majority of home network complaints.
Do not worry about pressing the reset hole on the back. Avoid it unless you are told to, since it erases the settings the provider installed.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a light pattern, and each pattern points at one thing.

items: No lights at all: check the socket and the adapter before calling anybody.
Power on and internet off: the provider's line is down. Call with the account number.
Internet light red: report a line fault, since it is not a setting in the house.
All lights on and no page loads: try another device, then another website.
The wifi light is off: somebody pressed the wifi button. Press it again.
The router restarts every hour: the adapter is failing, or it is overheating.

body.text: Practice
Learn your own lights, so a fault takes ten seconds.

items: Photograph the router while everything works, so you know the normal pattern.
Label each light with a small sticker and a word.
Practise the restart, timing it with a phone.
Move the router if it sits inside a closed cabinet.
Write the provider's number on the router's label.

body.text: You can now read a router at a glance. In the next lesson you will choose between wifi and a cable.

excerpt: When a cable beats wifi, how walls and distance weaken the signal, and the cheap fixes that reach the back room.

body.text: This lesson is about wifi and the cable under the table. You will learn when a cable is the better choice, why walls weaken a signal, and the cheap fixes that reach the far room.
Wifi is radio, and radio loses strength through walls and distance. A cable carries the signal without loss, which is why an older machine often works better plugged in.
Before you start

items: A device and the router.
A network cable if you have one.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: When a cable wins

items: For a desktop or a television that never moves.
For video calls, where a dropped signal ends the call.
For downloading large files, where speed matters.
For gaming, where delay is felt immediately.
For a room where the wifi shows one bar.
For security, since a cable cannot be joined from outside the house.

body.text: You will see the wifi icon become a small plug or a computer symbol when the cable is connected, and the connection stops wobbling. That steadiness is the whole benefit.
The wifi list will show a strength bar beside each network, and the bars in the far room tell you more than a speed test. Compare the bars in two rooms before buying anything.

body.alt: A laptop connected to a router by a network cable.
body.caption: A cable, a click, and no more dropped calls. Most routers have four ports and use two.

body.text: It looks like wifi has replaced cables entirely. A cable still carries the steadiest signal, and it costs less than any extender.
Why the signal fades

items: Each wall removes strength, especially a wall with metal or water pipes.
Distance matters more than the number of walls in most homes.
A microwave oven interferes while it is running.
A cordless phone base and a baby monitor can sit on the same frequency.
A router shut inside a cabinet is a router behind a metal door.
The 2.4 band travels further, and the 5 band is faster over a short distance.

body.text: A signal test will show a strength figure that drops by half in the next room. Walking the phone around the house while watching that figure finds the dead spots in two minutes.

body.alt: A router placed high in a sitting room away from walls.
body.caption: High, central, and out of any closed cabinet. Position changes the signal more than any setting.

body.text: Cheap fixes, in order

items: Move the router to a central, high place.
Point the antennae upward, not sideways.
Change the wifi channel if the app shows a crowded one.
Use the 2.4 band for the far rooms and the 5 band near the router.
Run a cable to the far room if the wall is the problem.
Add a second access point connected by cable, rather than a repeater.

body.text: None of this needs a technician. Moving the router and running one cable fixes more homes than a repeater ever does.
Do not worry about the cable looking untidy. A cable along a skirting board is less trouble than a call that drops every ten minutes.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a plain cause, and most are about position rather than equipment.

items: The far room has one bar: move the router first, then consider a cable.
The signal drops at the same time each evening: a neighbour's network or an appliance.
The cable is connected but nothing loads: the port may be off, so try another port.
The 5 band disappears in the next room: it is short range, which is normal.
The repeater halves the speed: it repeats rather than extends. Use a cable where you can.
The wifi is fine and one device is slow: the problem is that device's adapter.

body.text: Practice
Test one room before buying anything.

items: Walk the phone around the house, watching the signal strength.
Note the two weakest places.
Move the router higher and repeat the walk.
Connect one device by cable and compare the steadiness.
Write down which fix helped most.

body.text: You can now put the signal where you need it. In the next lesson you will work out what a megabyte actually buys.

excerpt: Bits, bytes, and the difference that doubles your bill: how much data a video, a song, and a page actually use.

body.text: This lesson explains what a megabyte is and where your data goes. You will learn the difference between bits and bytes, how much a video or a song uses, and how to plan a bundle that lasts the month.
A byte is a small unit of data, and a megabyte is a million of them. Providers sell bundles in megabytes or gigabytes, and they advertise speeds in megabits, which is one eighth of a megabyte.
Before you start

items: Your bundle size and its price.
The data usage screen on the phone.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Bits and bytes

items: A byte is written with a capital B, and a bit with a small b.
Eight bits make one byte, which is why the numbers differ by a factor of eight.
A speed of 10 Mbps is about 1.2 megabytes per second.
Downloading a 100 megabyte file at that speed takes about eighty seconds.
A bundle of 1.5 gigabytes is 1,500 megabytes, and it disappears quickly with video.
The phone's usage screen counts in megabytes, which is the figure that matches a bundle.

body.text: You will see the speed test report megabits while the file manager reports megabytes, and the two numbers will never match. That mismatch is units rather than a fault.

body.alt: A phone held in the hand showing a data usage figure.
body.caption: Megabytes used, in the hand. The figure is the one that tells you how long a bundle will last.

body.text: It looks like a bigger bundle costs less per megabyte. Often it does, and a bundle you do not finish is money spent rather than saved.
What things actually use

items: A text message: a few kilobytes, which is nothing.
A web page with photographs: one to three megabytes.
A song on a streaming service: about four megabytes.
A short video clip: ten to fifty megabytes, depending on quality.
An hour of standard video: three hundred to seven hundred megabytes.
An hour of high definition video: one to three gigabytes.

body.text: A usage screen will show a single evening of video as more than a week of messaging, which is the pattern worth remembering. Video is almost always the answer to where the bundle went.

body.alt: A laptop playing a video in the evening beside a phone.
body.caption: One evening of video can cost a week of everything else. Lower the quality and the bundle lasts.

body.text: Planning a bundle

items: Write the bundle size and the number of days it should cover.
Divide the megabytes by the days, which gives a daily allowance.
Check the daily figure against the usage screen for a normal day.
Choose the lower video quality in the apps you use most.
Download music and videos on wifi rather than streaming on data.
Buy the next bundle before the last one finishes, so you are not caught.
Review the month once, and change the size rather than the habit.

body.text: None of this needs a data app. The phone's own counter, a division, and one line in a notebook cover the whole plan.
Do not worry about counting every megabyte. Two habits, lower video quality and wifi downloads, change the month more than tracking does.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a plain explanation, and the usage screen is the evidence.

items: The bundle finished early: check video and hotspot use first.
The speed test is good and pages crawl: the site or the device is the slow part.
A 1 gigabyte bundle lasted two days: that is ordinary with an hour of video a day.
The phone shows more usage than the provider: the counts start on different days.
A download failed at ninety per cent: it will start again, and the data is spent.
An update used the data: the store was set to update on any network.

body.text: Practice
Work out one daily allowance.

items: Write the bundle size in megabytes.
Divide by the number of days it should last.
Compare with a normal day's usage.
Set the video quality to the lower option for a week.
Check the total again and compare.

body.text: You can now buy data with a plan rather than a hope. In the next lesson you will diagnose a network that has gone slow.

excerpt: A step-by-step diagnosis for a slow network: isolating the device, the router, and the line, and what to tell the provider when it is theirs.

body.text: This lesson is a diagnosis for a slow network. You will test one device, then the router, then the line, and know which of the three is at fault before you call anybody.
A slow connection has three possible homes: the device in your hand, the router in the house, and the line from the provider. Testing in that order takes five minutes and saves a wasted call.
Before you start

items: Two devices, one of them a phone.
The router's lights, visible.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Step one: one device

items: Try the same page on a phone and on the computer.
If one works and one does not, the fault is in that device.
Restart the device, which clears more than people expect.
Check the device's wifi signal strength in the same room as the router.
Close the tabs and programs you are not using.
Forget the network on the device and join it again.

body.text: You will see the working device load the same page normally, which rules out the line entirely. That single comparison is the most useful test in this lesson.

body.alt: A person crouching to check the lights on a router.
body.caption: Read the lights before the next test. A red internet light ends the diagnosis in ten seconds.

body.text: It looks like a slow page means a slow connection. One working device and one failing device describe a device problem, not a network one.
Step two: the router

items: Read the lights and note any that are off or red.
Switch it off at the wall, wait thirty seconds, and switch it on.
Wait two minutes without touching it.
Test one page on one device.
Check the wifi password has not been changed by somebody in the house.
Look at how many devices are connected, since twenty is different from three.

body.text: The router's device list will show every phone, television, and laptop attached, which often explains the evening slowdown. A guest who never left is a common finding.

body.alt: A phone showing a speed test result with download and upload figures.
body.caption: A speed test at the router and in the far room tells you whether the line or the wifi is the limit.

body.text: Step three: the line
If every device is slow, the problem is the line, and the provider needs specific information.

items: Run a speed test connected by cable, standing beside the router.
Run the same test in the far room, and compare the two figures.
Check whether a neighbour has the same problem at the same hour.
Note the times of day when it is worst, since busy hours are a real answer.
Photograph the router's lights while the fault is happening.
Call with the account number, the ticket number, and the two speed results.

body.text: None of this needs technical language. Two speed figures and a photograph of the lights are more useful to a support line than a description of how slow it feels.
Do not worry about being told to restart it again. Say that you have, and give the figures, which moves the conversation forward.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a cause, and each cause has a home.

items: One page fails and others load: the site is the problem, not your line.
Everything fails after a storm: check the wall box and call the provider.
The speed test is good and pages crawl: the name service is slow, so try a different one.
Only video buffers: the app's quality setting is too high for the line.
It slows at the same hour every evening: the network is busy, which is not a fault in the house.
The router drops the connection hourly: the adapter or the router is failing.

body.text: Practice
Run the three steps once, while everything works, so you know the numbers.

items: Run a speed test beside the router.
Run the same test in the furthest room.
Write both figures in your notebook, with the date.
Count the devices connected to the wifi.
Photograph the router's lights while it is healthy.

body.text: You can now tell a slow device from a slow line. In the next lesson you will look at how names are given to machines on a network.
